Plainly
plān'lĭ
adv. (clearly; without disguise or obscurity; in words that need no interpreter)
Latin planus, level, flat, clear. To speak plainly is to speak on level ground — nothing raised up to be climbed over, nothing hidden in a hollow.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The bondservant who chooses perpetual service must “plainly say, I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free” (Exo 21:5) — a life-altering commitment must be spoken in unmistakable words before witnesses. The law itself was to be published the same way: “thou shalt write upon the stones all the words of this law very plainly” (Deu 27:8), on plaistered stones at Ebal, where any Israelite could read them. God's dealings with men are described in the same terms: “Did I plainly appear unto the house of thy father, when they were in Egypt in Pharaoh's house?” (1Sa 2:27), the man of God to Eli, arguing from a revelation that had not been obscure. And plainness can be selective: Saul told his uncle plainly that the asses were found, “but of the matter of the kingdom, whereof Samuel spake, he told him not” (1Sa 10:16). In the New Testament the Lord tells the disciples plainly that Lazarus is dead, and speaks of the hour when He shall shew them plainly of the Father; and Paul makes plainness a matter of ministerial conscience: we use great plainness of speech, and are not as many, which corrupt the word of God.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines plainly as without gloss or disguise; clearly; evidently; in a manner to be easily understood; frankly; honestly.

expand to see more

PLAINLY, adv. Without glosses or disguise; honestly; sincerely.

2. In a manner to be easily seen or comprehended.

3. Frankly; candidly; without reserve; as, tell me plainly what you think.

Key Scripture

Deu 27:8 — "And thou shalt write upon the stones all the words of this law very plainly."

Exo 21:5 — "And if the servant shall plainly say, I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free:"

2Co 3:12 — "Seeing then that we have such hope, we use great plainness of speech:"

Modern Corruption

Preaching that leaves the hearer uncertain what was claimed is now often praised as thoughtful, and Scripture treats plainness as a duty of the messenger rather than a defect of style.

expand to see more

Deuteronomy 27:8 is a small command with a large principle: write it very plainly. The stones at Ebal were plaistered and inscribed so that the law could be read by farmers and shepherds standing in a field, not decoded by a class of interpreters. That is the Bible's own instinct about its own words, and it is the doctrine the Reformers called the perspicuity of Scripture — not that every passage is equally easy, which the Confession expressly denies, but that the things necessary to be known, believed and observed for salvation are so clearly propounded that not only the learned but the unlearned, in a due use of ordinary means, may attain a sufficient understanding of them. Two opposite corruptions attack it. The older is the priestly one, which keeps the text in a language the people cannot read and reserves its meaning to a hierarchy; the Reformation answered it with translation. The newer is a habit of preaching and writing in which nothing is ever quite asserted — the sermon raises questions, offers perspectives, and closes without the hearer being able to say what the preacher claimed — and this is often mistaken for humility and depth. Paul's standard is plainness of speech, and he grounds it in confidence rather than arrogance: seeing then that we have such hope, we use great plainness of speech. A man who is sure of his message can afford to be understood.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ba'ar (H874), to make plain, to engrave distinctly; Greek parrhesia (G3954), freedom of speech, boldness, plainness; Greek saphos, clearly.

expand to see more

Hebrew ba'ar (H874) — to make distinct, to engrave plainly; the law on the stones at Ebal, and the vision written that he may run that readeth it; Deuteronomy 27:8, Habakkuk 2:2.

Greek parrhesia (G3954) — all-speech, freedom to say everything; rendered plainness, boldness, and confidence, of the apostles and of the believer's access; 2 Corinthians 3:12, Acts 4:13, Hebrews 4:16.

Hebrew infinitive absolute construction — the doubling that gives “plainly say” and “plainly appear” their emphatic force; Exodus 21:5, 1 Samuel 2:27.

Usage

"“Write upon the stones all the words of this law very plainly” — readable in a field."

"“If the servant shall plainly say” — a life-altering choice spoken in unmistakable words."

"“We use great plainness of speech” — plainness grounded in confidence."
